title: Fertility is a valid policy concern | Institute for Family Studies
gist: In The Carolina Journal, John Hood argues that policymakers should care about fertility. North Carolina's fertility rate is well below replacement, and the state grows only through migration from other states and countries. He notes that US fertility has moved in cycles historically but is now at record lows.

insights.claim: North Carolina's fertility rate is well below replacement level, and its population still grows only because people move in from other states and countries.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Growth that depends on migration is fragile: housing, labor-force and tax-base forecasts depend on inflows continuing rather than on births.
insights.quote: North Carolina’s fertility rate is currently well below replacement level. Our population continues to grow because we’re importing people from other states and countries.

insights.claim: US fertility has moved in cycles: it fell through most of the 19th and early 20th centuries, rebounded in the 1940s-50s Baby Boom, fell until the mid-1970s, recovered somewhat in the late 20th and early 21st centuries, and is now at record lows.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Fertility has rebounded before, so the current low is not necessarily permanent, but it is the lowest on record.

insights.so_what: Falling TFR across countries points to slower labor-force growth and more pressure on pension systems.
